nameStory: The Furrow Orbweaver gets its name from the distinctive pattern on its abdomen that looks remarkably like the deep grooves a farmer's plow leaves in a field. These leaf-like markings, called foliate patterns, create ridges and valleys across the spider's back that catch light and shadow just like freshly tilled earth. It's also sometimes called the foliate spider for these same leafy, textured markings.
description: The Furrow Orbweaver is a robust, medium-sized spider that's one of our most common orb weavers in New England. Its most striking feature is the intricate pattern of ridges and furrows running down its plump abdomen, creating a textured appearance that looks almost carved or embossed. The spider typically displays mottled brown, gray, and sometimes orange coloring that helps it blend perfectly with tree bark. Adults are chunky and substantial-feeling spiders that build classic circular webs.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Look for the signature furrow pattern on the abdomen - raised ridges and deep grooves that feel bumpy if gently touched, creating a textured surface like corduroy fabric

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Stocky, robust build with a noticeably plump, rounded abdomen that's much wider than the narrow front section (cephalothorax)

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates classic circular orb webs, often with the spider sitting head-down in the center or hiding nearby in a silken retreat

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized spider with females having bodies about the size of a large pea, males noticeably smaller and more slender

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often rebuilds web nightly, and when disturbed will drop on a silk line or curl up and play dead

habitat: Furrow Orbwevers thrive around human structures, building webs on porches, decks, window frames, and outdoor lights throughout New England. They also inhabit forest edges, gardens, and areas where trees meet open spaces. You'll often spot their webs strung between fence posts, shrubs, or in the corners of buildings where they can anchor their circular webs securely.

seasonality.spring: Young spiders emerge and begin building small webs. Look for tiny versions of the adult pattern already visible on their abdomens.
seasonality.summer: Peak web-building season with large, perfect circular webs most visible in early morning dew. Adults reach full size and mating occurs.
seasonality.fall: Females lay egg sacs and webs become most noticeable as vegetation dies back. Adults remain active until first hard frost.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off but egg sacs overwinter in protected crevices. Webs disappear but you might find old silk remnants on structures.

funFact: Furrow Orbweavers are like eight-legged recycling machines - they eat their entire web every morning and rebuild it fresh each night, consuming and reusing every strand of silk in an endless cycle of demolition and construction.
confusionNotes: Often confused with other brown orbweavers, but the furrow pattern is your key - run your eyes along the abdomen looking for those distinctive ridges and grooves. Think 'plowed field' and you'll remember to look for the textured, furrowed appearance that sets this species apart from smoother-bodied relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their robust appearance and prominent webs around homes, Furrow Orbweavers are completely harmless to humans. Like all orbweavers, they can bite if handled roughly, but their bites typically cause only mild, temporary discomfort similar to a mosquito bite.
compareHints: Furrow Orbweavers are distinguished from their Larinioides cousins by their pronounced textured abdomen pattern. The Grey Cross Spider has a smoother body with a distinct cross marking, while the Ornamental Orbweaver tends to be more colorful with different patterning. The furrow pattern is unique to this species - if you see those distinctive ridges and grooves, you've found your spider.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its cousin the Furrow Orbweaver which prefers vegetation and natural settings, the Grey Cross Spider is the urbanite of the genus, almost exclusively choosing metal structures and artificial lights.
Compared to the Furrow Orbweaver in the same genus, Ornamental Orbweavers typically display more complex and variable abdominal patterns rather than the simple central furrow.
